title: Karuna as a subject
hookLine: an odd instruction: feel compassion even for a wrongdoer who is happy right now
tomorrow: is the opposite of being glad for someone envy, or boredom?

cards: Somebody's posts are all wins: the trip, the new car, the big news. And somewhere in the comments, they're cutting other people down. Compassion is the last thing that comes up.
Yet the Visuddhimagga has an odd instruction. If you can't find anyone suffering to practice on, it says, feel compassion for a wrongdoer, even one who's happy right now.
Why would anyone need compassion while they're winning?

teach.b: The manual answers with a picture. A man has been caught stealing and is being led away to be punished. Along the road, people hand him sweets and flowers, and he enjoys them.
Nobody watching thinks he's lucky. They can see where the road goes. Someone causing harm, the manual says, is on that road too, laughing or not: his actions are walking him somewhere hard.
Karuna, compassion, looks past the moment.

As a meditation subject it starts with someone plainly suffering, so the heart opens easily. Then, as with metta, it widens: someone dear, someone neutral, someone hostile. And the manual names two enemies.
The far enemy is cruelty, which is obvious.
The near enemy is sneakier, because it looks like compassion from a distance: a sorrow that just sits in the sadness and sinks.
Karuna isn't sinking. It's the steady wish that the pain end. That's why it can reach a person who's winning right now and still be gentle.

how: Compassion meditation is practiced across Buddhist traditions; in the Visuddhimagga's method it begins with someone clearly suffering and widens to dear, neutral and hostile people.

games.q: what does “karuna as a subject” mean?
o: feeling sad along with anyone who's sad
forgiving someone who has hurt you badly
wishing that someone's suffering would end

games.q: compassion and its enemies — tap the pairs.
p: fed sweets, but nobody envies him

s: compassion is only for people who are visibly suffering
the manual stretches it even to a wrongdoer who looks happy, like the man fed sweets on the road.
in the manual, compassion's near enemy is cruelty
cruelty is the far enemy; the near one is a sorrow that just sits in sadness.
compassion practice starts with someone plainly suffering
so the heart opens easily; then it widens to dear, neutral and hostile people.

games.q: a guy in your class mocks everyone and always seems thrilled about it. your friend says he deserves zero sympathy. what does the manual's road picture suggest?
o: he's having fun, so there's no suffering there to feel for.
compassion: his actions are walking him somewhere hard.
feel sorry for him and stay sad about it until he changes.
games.why: the man on the road was enjoying sweets, and nobody thought him lucky. compassion looks past the moment, and it wishes, without sinking.

practice: Place a hand over your heart and bring to mind someone who is struggling right now. With each out-breath, silently wish: may you be free of this. If sadness starts to pull you down, come back to the wish itself, light and steady.

wordCard.voice: Karuna as a subject: compassion made the object of meditation. The steady wish that someone's suffering end, reaching even people who look fine.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: compassion, the wish that suffering end.

carryVoice: The line to keep: compassion, for the ones who look fine too. Day thirty of the forty.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 9 (compassion: begin with a person in misery; compassion for an evil-doer though happy, with the simile of a caught thief led to execution and given food on the way; near enemy grief, far enemy cruelty)
